scenario: AITA in relation to my GF's attempt to lose weight? | I've been dating my GF for 3 years. She's upset at her current weight. She's put on about 100lbs since we started dating. I've never mentioned it because she has bipolar disorder, and as I struggle with depression I fully understand how food can take the edge off when you get seriously overwhelmed with depression. But for health reasons and of course other reasons, of course I would like for her to get back to a healthy weight. My girlfriend's bipolar disorder has been a challenge for me, as where I would normally be assertive in a relationship on issues - I often have to back down in arguments because she responds poorly to being challenged. I often feel like I'm walking on ice, but I do my best to try understand her and work at helping her and supporting her as best I can. She is not happy with her current weight, and constantly remarks about it and has been complaining about it for over a year without doing anything about it. I tell her we can work on it together as a team, and both fix our diet. I feel this is the best way to go about it, rather than telling her that SHE needs to lose weight. I don't want her feeling like I'm initiating it, or that it's a journey she needs to take alone. Or that I'm pushing her to do it. For it to be a healthy journey, it needs to be something she is motivated to do and if I do it with her, then it doesn't feel like it's all on her. So, last week she decided to work on her diet. She was upset today because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I told her to not worry about the short term results - that it had only been a week, but to focus on months down the line to see changes. She was extremely defeatist and said she'll never lose weight. This kinda irritated me, because it had only been a week since she started. I felt like she hadn't fully committed, because she was drinking soft drinks and eating chips which are high in carbs so I brought that up, if she wants to see results quicker - that cutting out the junk food completely (rather than cutting down) will help her. Now I understand she's trying to make a change, but the defeatist attitude after only a week is difficult to work with. She then got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight". To which I replied that I wasn't, I had never in our entire relationship brought up her weight, and was just discussing her diet and how she was eating and drinking things that will make her progress slower. She then told me to drop it and leave it alone, and is now in a huff with me for the past few hours over it. I understand this is the nature of her bipolar disorder, and she will shut down anything she's challenged about something. Am I the asshole for challenging her defeatist attitude on her results, when she was taking short-cuts with junk food?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being an asshole in this situation with my girlfriend. Let me start by laying out the details as I understand them. We've been dating for three years, and she's been struggling with her weight, having gained about 100 pounds since we started dating. I know she has bipolar disorder, and I've been through depression myself, so I get how food can be a coping mechanism when you're overwhelmed. I've never mentioned her weight because I don't want to make her feel bad or trigger her condition. But I'm concerned about her health and would like her to get back to a healthy weight. She's expressed her own unhappiness about her weight and has been talking about it for over a year without taking action. I suggested that we work on our diet together as a team, thinking that if we do it together, it won't feel like it's all on her. I wanted to support her and make it a joint effort rather than something she has to do alone. Last week, she decided to start working on her diet. But today, she was upset because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I tried to reassure her that it's only been a week and that she should focus on the long-term changes. I told her not to worry about the short-term results. However, she became very defeatist, saying she'll never lose weight. That frustrated me because I felt like she wasn't fully committed, especially since she was still drinking sodas and eating chips, which are high in carbs. I brought up that if she wants to see quicker results, she should cut out junk food completely instead of just cutting down. I explained that I was just discussing her diet and how her eating habits were affecting her progress, not her weight. But she got angry, told me to stop arguing about her weight, and then shut down the conversation, leaving me feeling like I was the asshole. Now, I'm wondering if I overstepped by challenging her defeatist attitude, especially when she was taking shortcuts with junk food. I understand her bipolar disorder makes her sensitive to being challenged, but I also feel like I was trying to support her in a healthy way. Let me break this down. On one hand, I was trying to help her by suggesting changes that could lead to better results. I wanted to encourage her to commit fully to the diet so she could see progress. On the other hand, I might have come across as pushy or critical, which could have triggered her. She has a history of shutting down when she feels challenged, so maybe I should have been more sensitive to that. I also need to consider her feelings. She's already upset about her weight and hasn't seen results yet. My frustration might have made her feel unsupported or criticized, even if that wasn't my intention. Maybe I should have approached the conversation differently, focusing on her feelings and offering support without pushing for specific changes. I wonder if there's a better way to handle this. Perhaps I could have acknowledged her feelings of defeat and frustration first before bringing up the junk food. Maybe something like, "I understand you're feeling discouraged, and it's okay to feel that way. Let's see how we can adjust our approach to make this easier for you." That way, I'm validating her emotions before offering suggestions. Also, I should think about the timing. She was already upset, so bringing up the junk food might have been adding fuel to the fire. Maybe it's better to wait until she's calmer to discuss any changes in diet. I also need to reflect on my own feelings. I'm concerned about her health, but I don't want that to come across as criticism. It's a delicate balance between supporting her and encouraging her to make healthy choices without making her feel like she's being judged. In the end, I think I might have been too direct in my approach, not considering how she would react given her bipolar disorder. While my intentions were good, the way I presented the feedback might have been insensitive. I should have been more empathetic and perhaps less focused on the specifics of her diet at that moment. So, considering all this, I think I might have been the asshole in this situation by not being as sensitive as I could have been to her emotional state and the way she reacts to being challenged. I should work on approaching these conversations with more empathy and understanding, especially given her condition.
